category.name: AI Security
category.description: Threat modeling for LLM and ML systems: prompt injection, data exfiltration, tool abuse and training-data risk.

lab.title: Customer Support AI Agent
lab.summary: An LLM agent that answers customer questions and can act on their account through internal tools.
lab.businessContext: A SaaS company is deploying an AI support agent that can read documentation and take account actions on the customer's behalf.
lab.systemContext: A chat widget reaches an agent service, which retrieves from a document index, calls an LLM provider, and invokes internal tools that read and modify customer accounts.

nodes.label: Agent Service
nodes.description: Orchestrates retrieval, model calls and tool use

nodes.label: Document Index
nodes.description: Embedded help articles and internal runbooks

architectureIssues.title: The model chooses which account a tool acts on
architectureIssues.description: Tool calls carry an account identifier produced by the model rather than one bound to the authenticated session.
architectureIssues.hint: Where does the account id in the tool call actually come from?

architectureIssues.title: Untrusted user text and trusted runbooks share one prompt
architectureIssues.description: Retrieved internal documents and the customer's own message are concatenated with no delimitation or trust marking.
architectureIssues.hint: How does the model know which part of its input is an instruction?

architectureIssues.title: Internal runbooks sit in the same index as public help articles
architectureIssues.description: The retrieval index mixes customer-facing documentation with internal procedures and no audience filter is described.
architectureIssues.hint: What is the worst thing retrieval could surface into a customer's chat?

architectureIssues.title: Tools have no described scope or rate limit
architectureIssues.description: Nothing constrains which actions the agent may take, how often, or which are irreversible.
architectureIssues.hint: Should an agent be able to issue a thousand refunds?

architectureIssues.title: Ticket history loaded without tenant scoping
architectureIssues.description: Past conversations are retrieved as context with no stated restriction to the current customer.
architectureIssues.hint: Whose previous conversations end up in this prompt?

threats.title: Prompt injection escalates into unauthorised account actions
threats.description: A customer instructs the model to act on a different account. Because the tool call takes its account id from the model's output, the instruction becomes a real privileged action.
threats.learnerExplanation: Prompt injection is only as dangerous as the permissions behind the model.

threats.title: Internal runbooks surfaced to a customer
threats.description: Retrieval pulls an internal procedure into the answer, disclosing internal processes, thresholds or credentials to an outsider.
threats.learnerExplanation: Everything in the index is reachable by anyone who can phrase the right question.

threats.title: Another customer's conversation appears as context
threats.description: Unscoped history retrieval leaks one customer's support conversation, and its personal data, into another's chat.
threats.learnerExplanation: Multi-tenant retrieval needs the tenant filter in the query, not in the prompt.

threats.title: Customer personal data sent to a third-party model provider
threats.description: Full account context and conversation history leave the platform on every call, with no stated minimisation or retention agreement.
threats.learnerExplanation: The provider boundary is a real trust boundary.

threats.title: Unbounded tool invocation causes financial or operational damage
threats.description: With no rate limit or human gate on irreversible actions, a manipulated agent can issue mass refunds or bulk changes.
threats.learnerExplanation: Agents act at machine speed; blast radius matters more than intent.

mitigations.title: Bind every tool call to the authenticated session
mitigations.description: Take the account id from the server-side session, never from model output, and reject any tool call that names a different account.

mitigations.title: Audience-scoped retrieval index
mitigations.description: Tag every document with its audience and filter to customer-visible content before retrieval.

mitigations.title: Tenant filter applied in the retrieval query
mitigations.description: Constrain history and index lookups by tenant at the query layer so cross-tenant results cannot be returned.

mitigations.title: Minimise and redact before calling the provider
mitigations.description: Strip identifiers not needed for the answer and contract for zero retention.

mitigations.title: Scoped tools with rate limits and human approval
mitigations.description: Allow-list actions, cap frequency, and require human confirmation for anything irreversible.

mitigations.title: Add 'ignore malicious instructions' to the system prompt
mitigations.description: A worthwhile layer, but prompt text alone cannot be relied on to stop injection reaching a privileged tool.

mitigations.title: Profanity filter on model output
mitigations.description: Improves tone; irrelevant to every threat in this system.

threatMitigations.explanation: If the account is fixed by the session, a successful injection still cannot reach another customer.
Content that is never retrieved cannot be surfaced by any prompt.
Filtering at the query layer makes cross-tenant results structurally impossible.
Data that never leaves cannot be retained or exposed by the provider.
Scope, rate limits and human gates bound the damage a manipulated agent can do.

releaseGuidance.rationale: The critical finding is architectural: the agent takes the account identifier for privileged tool calls from model output, which turns any successful prompt injection into a real action on someone else's account. Prompt injection is not reliably preventable, so the correct posture is to assume it succeeds and ensure it cannot reach authority — which this design does not. Hardening the system prompt is not a fix. Combined with unscoped retrieval leaking internal runbooks and other tenants' conversations, this is not a launchable configuration. A read-only agent with no tools would be shippable with conditions.
suggestedConditions: Bind all tool calls to the authenticated session; never accept an account id from the model.
Apply tenant and audience filters at the retrieval query layer.
Separate internal runbooks from the customer-facing index.
Minimise and redact data before it reaches the model provider.
Add rate limits and human approval for irreversible actions.
